children: Starbucks (NASDAQ:SBUX) CEO Brian Niccol says the coffee giant has moved beyond stabilizing its business and entered the next phase of its turnaround, with renovated stores, faster service and a renewed focus on customer connections driving the recovery.
Starbucks is back. Our business has made the turn, Niccol told employees in a memo discussed during an exclusive CNBC interview Thursday.

Two years after taking charge, Niccol said the shine is back on Starbucks and credited employees with embracing his Back to Starbucks strategy. CNBC noted that the stock had risen about 10% since his first day as CEO and roughly 30% since his appointment was announced.

Niccol inherited a chain facing complaints about long mobile-order waits, labor problems and elevated prices. His response centered on investing in employees and coffeehouses while tightening standards governing drink quality and order speed.
The turnaround is not finished, however.

Starbucks is about nine months into its store-uplift program and has already renovated well over 1,000 coffeehouses. Niccol expects that total to reach at least 1,500 by the end of the company's fiscal year, followed by upgrades at thousands of additional locations during the next fiscal year.
The projects are designed to restore comfortable seating, warmth and the familiar atmosphere that traditionally distinguished Starbucks from more transactional restaurant concepts.

Niccol is also pushing the company's Green Apron service model, which focuses on appropriate staffing, effective employee deployment and stronger support inside stores. The objective is to make each customer interaction not a transaction, but a moment.
That could mean greeting customers as they enter, writing a small note on a cup or creating a more personal handoff when an order is ready.

Starbucks has also installed digital menu boards across nearly all its coffeehouses, giving the chain greater flexibility to promote different products throughout the day. Morning displays can emphasize breakfast sandwiches, hot and cold coffee, and protein cold foam, while later menus can adapt to changing customer demand.
Niccol specifically highlighted protein cold foam and recommended the pumpkin version, which Starbucks promoted with Martha Stewart during its seasonal pumpkin-spice launch.

For investors, Niccol's declaration marks an important shift in the turnaround narrative. Starbucks is no longer focused exclusively on repairing obvious operational problems. Its next test is whether thousands of store renovations, better staffing and more flexible merchandising can produce a consistently stronger customer experience across the chain.

title: Brian Niccol Doubles Down on Starbucks Comeback
